title: Shopping
goal: Ask prices, bargain and pay — while picking up *duit*, *ringgit*, *sen* and the whole set of colors, sizes and counting words used in shops.
bekal: ask the price and bargain without sounding rude
talk about size, color and number of items with the right classifier
read Malaysian shop signs: *jualan murah*, *diskaun*, *tukar*, *bayar di kaunter*

notes: **Berapa harga ni?** ("how-much price this?") is the most common way to ask a price in Malaysia. Other common forms: *Ni berapa?* (this, how much?) and *Berapa satu?* (how much each?).

**Mahalnya!** — *-nya* on the end of an adjective makes an **exclamation**, not a possessive. *Mahalnya!* = "So expensive!", *Cantiknya!* = "How pretty!", *Panasnya!* = "It's so hot!". Malaysians use it constantly.

**Boleh kurang tak?** ("can less, or not?") is the standard bargaining line. Others: *Kurang sikit boleh?*, *Ada diskaun tak?*, *Harga last berapa?* (what's your last price?). Bargaining is normal at night markets and street markets; in mall shops and supermarkets it is **not**.
**Alah** is a half-hearted "oh, all right then" — the sound of giving in. Its cousins: *aiya*, *ala*, *ish*.
**Takde** is the spoken form of *tak ada* / *tiada* (there isn't). *Takde bilik cuba* = there's no fitting room. You'll hear it all the time; the formal form **tiada** mostly appears in writing.

grammars.title: Duit, ringgit, sen — and how to say prices
body: Malaysia's currency is the **ringgit** (RM), divided into **sen**. One ringgit = 100 sen. Prices are written with a decimal **point**, just as in English.
after: Good news: **commas and points work exactly as in English** — RM1,200.50 is one thousand two hundred ringgit fifty sen. (⚠️ Indonesia swaps them: Rp1.200,50. If a price ever looks a thousand times off, check the marks.)
**Duit** and **wang** both mean money. *Duit* is everyday (like "cash"), *wang* is more formal and used at banks and on forms. The Indonesian word *uang* **isn't used** in Malaysia.

grammars.title: Classifiers — counting words
body: English has a few counting words — "a **piece** of paper", "a **pair** of shoes", "two **head** of cattle". Standard Malay uses them for almost everything you count, and a wrong one is noticed at once.
after: Note the attached **se-**: *sebuah*, *seorang*, *sehelai*, *secawan* — it means "one" (or "a") and is written as one word.

⚠️ In everyday speech Malaysians often drop the classifier: *dua baju*, *tiga kopi*. That's fine in conversation. But in **writing**, school essays and forms, the right classifier is expected — which is why it's still taught.

blocks.text: Three colors to note: **kelabu** (grey), **perang** (brown — ⚠️ in Indonesian *perang* means war!) and **merah jambu** (pink, literally "rose-apple red"). And "thin" is **nipis**.

For dark and light shades, Malay puts **gelap** (dark) and **cerah/muda** (light, "young") after the color: *biru gelap* (dark blue), *hijau muda* (light green). Colors, like all adjectives, come **after** the noun: *baju hitam* = a black shirt.
Four words to learn now: **seluar** (trousers), **kasut** (shoes), **cermin mata** (glasses, "mirror eyes") and **baju sejuk** (sweater, "cold shirt"). All four are used every day.

sections.title: Where to shop and the signs you'll see

blocks.title: Signs you'll see
items: **BELI 1 PERCUMA 1** — buy one, get one free. (⚠️ *percuma* = free)
**BAYAR DI KAUNTER** — pay at the counter.

blocks.text: The word **kecemasan** means **emergency**. *Pintu kecemasan* = emergency exit, *bilik kecemasan* = the hospital emergency room. (Indonesian *kecemasan* means "anxiety", so Indonesian visitors often misread this sign.)
